bp-graph.title: The record, and 17 questions of it
bp-graph.tip: The graph is what the loop believes. Each criterion is one question asked of it, named for the mistake it would catch. A hole of ours fails the run; a hole of the owner's is a question.

bp-stats.title: The stats choose what's next
bp-stats.tip: Each pass measures itself. A stat nothing reads is a cost with no use, and the audit says so. The same shape sits one level up, where stats are the code, triggers the requirements and ticks the tests.

bp-tick.title: The standing tick
bp-tick.tip: A fresh agent with no memory, one item, the same stat measured before and after. Nothing starts a tick for you; schedule one or don't.

bp-learned.title: What learns, and has to earn it
bp-learned.tip: A graph network that proposes links, a small model that predicts which breaks get past the tests, and a list of goals. Each is measured against a plain rule on data it never saw, and stays off if it loses.

bp-measure.title: Does it help? On against off
bp-measure.tip: The honest measure. Two agents get the same prompt and only one gets the loop. The harness measures what they made, and graders who cannot see which is which judge it.

bp-ship.title: Shipping it
bp-ship.tip: The kit other developers install, and the public pages. A possible leak fails the build rather than warning about it.

bp-agents.title: Many agents at once
bp-agents.tip: The runtime underneath. Agents share a project through files, not a server, and a stuck worker asks instead of guessing. who.py says who is on what, from their own transcripts.

tree.label: The guided tour
tree.tip: One real thread through the graph, from where a requirement comes from to the test that caught a break of it.

children.label: 1. The whole graph
children.tip: 1,729 nodes and 10,069 edges. Top to bottom: why it exists, what the code does, what proves it. Every point is a row the loop wrote.

children.label: 2. Where it comes from
children.tip: A requirement has to come from somewhere it can be checked against: here, a named source.

children.label: 3. The requirement
children.tip: A requirement, a node of its own. Everything below hangs off it.

children.label: 4. The step that needs it
children.tip: A use case step binds it into a chain of cause and effect.

children.label: 5. Claude's reasoning
children.tip: One step of a written argument. It cites the requirement and the code, and the graph checks those two really are joined.

children.label: 6. The code
children.tip: A method, a node of its own. The reasoning cites it by name, and a name the code does not have fails the run.

children.label: 7. One decision
children.tip: A branch of that method, and the requirement that owns it. This link is how code maps to requirements.

children.label: 8. Broken on purpose
children.tip: One break of that decision. It runs alone against the tests, and one of them has to fail.

children.label: 9. Caught
children.tip: The test that caught it failed when this break ran. That is the requirement being held.

children.label: 10. And one that got past
children.tip: No test caught this break. Either it changes nothing, and that has to be proven, or a test is missing.

children.label: 11. The readers
children.tip: Each large node outside the rings is one thing the harness tries to learn: 10 goals, 5 of them trained. Its rays go to what it reads. Solid has reached its goal, hollow has not, and a core in a shell is part way there or in doubt.

children.label: 12. Trying is not reaching
children.tip: Goal: who owns new code. It is trying, and it has not got there. The score below is against the plain rule it has to beat.

children.label: 13. The whole graph
children.tip: Fly anywhere: drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, W A S D to move. Point at a node to see what kind it is.

children.label: The agent at work
children.tip: What an agent does when someone asks it for a change. The tools below hold it to account; this sheet is the part only an agent can do.

children.label: One pass
children.tip: One command runs all of it, in this order. The numbers on the nodes come from a real pass on the kit's example, a small wallet and store in C#.

children.label: Breaking the code
children.tip: A coverage tool says a line ran. This asks whether any test would notice if the line were wrong. It never touches the live project; it works in a sandbox.

children.label: The requirements, as data
children.tip: The owner's words become a model a machine can check. Nothing here looks at whether the code works yet; this tests the requirements themselves.

children.label: The record, and 17 questions of it
children.tip: The graph is what the loop believes. Each criterion is one question asked of it, named for the mistake it would catch. A hole of ours fails the run; a hole of the owner's is a question.

children.label: The stats choose what's next
children.tip: Each pass measures itself. A stat nothing reads is a cost with no use, and the audit says so. The same shape sits one level up, where stats are the code, triggers the requirements and ticks the tests.

children.label: The standing tick
children.tip: A fresh agent with no memory, one item, the same stat measured before and after. Nothing starts a tick for you; schedule one or don't.

children.label: What learns, and has to earn it
children.tip: A graph network that proposes links, a small model that predicts which breaks get past the tests, and a list of goals. Each is measured against a plain rule on data it never saw, and stays off if it loses.

children.label: Does it help? On against off
children.tip: The honest measure. Two agents get the same prompt and only one gets the loop. The harness measures what they made, and graders who cannot see which is which judge it.

children.label: Shipping it
children.tip: The kit other developers install, and the public pages. A possible leak fails the build rather than warning about it.

children.label: Many agents at once
children.tip: The runtime underneath. Agents share a project through files, not a server, and a stuck worker asks instead of guessing. who.py says who is on what, from their own transcripts.

Slide 6 of 28: Requirements make requirements

It extracts new requirements from the ones you have

The words on this slide

Requirements make requirements

It extracts new requirements from the ones you have

Automatic

Each use case step needs something. What no requirement provides becomes a new one, marked inferred, and goes to the owner as a question.

Complete in, accurate out

The more complete the requirements, the more accurate the prompt built from them. Start with the ones that run through the most code.

Epic to code: not measured

The aim is a rough epic grown into a larger set, then code written from it. These trials started from a spec or a game’s own docs. The epic-to-code test has not run.

Behind: osu!’s requirements and use cases: one epic, four use cases, 30 requirements. We wrote all 30; the walk inferred none.

How requirements make requirements

6

What the speaker says

The tool’s main intent is to take the requirements for a game from a rough epic use case and grow them into a larger set, so that the code written from them is as accurate as it can be. The first card is the mechanism: it walks each use case, and when a step needs a condition that nothing provides, it marks an inferred requirement and sends it to the owner as a question, never as a decision. The second card is our judgment from building with it; no run has measured it directly. The third is the honest state. The trials on public code started from a published spec or from a game’s own doc comments, so their requirements were written from existing words: on osu! all 30 were written and none inferred, and on SemVer 3 of 19 are marked inferred. The end-to-end test, a rough epic grown into requirements and code written from them, graded by tests from an independent source, has not run: the last slide says what it would take. Two earlier tries give no number to lean on: growing a model from three requirements tied with and without the loop, and when two features of ours were joined the walk did not find the places they meet. This is the actual graph of osu!’s scoring rules, the rules of a shipped rhythm game (ppy/osu, MIT licence), drawn from the store the loop wrote: 1,062 nodes and 5,675 edges, nothing invented and nothing left out. The words on this slide

The record

The graph remembers; closed means no “may” is left

MUST

Authored requirements

The owner wrote them. Each must hold, and a test must notice when it does not.

MAY

Inferred requirements

What the chain needs and nobody wrote. Only the owner settles each one.

Breaking code can refute closure, never prove it: closed is always relative to the breaks tried and the tests that watch.

The graph, and must and may, in plain words

What the speaker says

The graph is the record, and the criteria read it. The closest formal idea of closed is the Modal Transition System of Larsen and Thomsen, 1988: every behaviour is marked must or may, and a specification is refined until no may is left. Here the authored requirements are the musts, and the inferred ones the chain needs are the mays. The owner's open questions are exactly those mays. Behind this slide: Inside the graph.

An owner's question no step reached is listed as a blind spot; this chain never reached W-4, what a refused purchase does to the stock. The step and the picture are from the kit's example, which you can run yourself: the chain was added to a copy of it and the whole loop run, and it held. How it works

Reads. Each node starts as its own words, hashed to 512 numbers.

From a rough epic to code that is right

The words on this slide

What is next

From a rough epic to code that is right

What the tool is for

Take the requirements for a game from a rough epic use case, grow them into a larger set, and write the code from that set as accurately as we can measure.

The question

If the requirements for something very difficult are complete and checked, how far does that move what an AI can build?

Measured so far

How much of existing code its tests hold: 87.3%, 69.7% and 53.4% of breaks caught on three public targets. In a control run on two of them, an agent reading carefully found as many faults as the loop did.

NOT MEASURED

The epic-to-code test has not run. Nothing yet shows that more requirements make the code more accurate.

The direction is better tools for making video games. It is not a claim about general intelligence.

What is measured, and what is not

28

What the speaker says

The tool’s main intent is to take the requirements for a game from a rough epic use case and grow them into a larger set, so that the code written from them is as accurate as it can be. The question on the right is a question and not a result: if we have the requirements to do something very difficult, how does that change the landscape for the AI? What is measured is narrower. On three public targets, a version parser, a JSON object and a game’s scoring rules, it measures how much of existing code its tests hold, and that held up against careful reading: a control run gave agents the same task with and without the loop, and blind graders found no real fault in only one arm. What is not measured is the thing the intent names. No rough epic has been grown into requirements and then into code, and no code written from grown requirements has been graded. The trials here started from a published spec or a game’s own doc comments, and a first try at growing a model from three requirements tied with and without the loop. The test we plan starts from one rough epic for a small game whose right answers come from an independent published source, such as published move-count tables for chess. Agents write the code with and without the grown requirements, and hidden tests written from that source, never from our model, grade both blind. Tokens per arm are recorded, and so are how many requirements the epic grew into and how many the hidden tests needed that it missed. The direction is more advanced tools for making video games, and not general intelligence.

So far

  • Graph network reached its goal on 1 of 6 results; small model on the break's features reached its goal on 4 of 4 results (2 of them doubted) (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • 3 of 10 results change with the random seed alone, so no single run settles one (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • Giving a goal more of the graph to read helped by more than the bar in 0 of 6 tries (an anecdote: 6 results).
  • Goals where each answer belongs to about one source, in a sparse table, beat a plain rule far more often than the rest. That says where plain rules are weak, not where work is saved (right 80% of the time against a 48% base, on 44 goals across 5 graphs, and 6 of 7 on goals sealed before they ran (an anecdote at that size)).
  • No rule was found that picks the goals which save work. All 60 of the best candidates were chance or anecdote (52 goals with a measured saving, across 5 domains).
  • Ordering tests by a plain rule already saves most of what ordering them can. A learned order beat it on only 2 of 10 goals (10 goals, 31% against 33% saved).
  • The graph offers these next, relations nothing predicts yet: checked by (110 links), asserts (30 links), next step (26 links), stated by (24 links), cites (21 links).

concept-goals.head:
The goals

The readers

Each large node outside the rings is one thing the loop tries to learn: 10 goals, 5 of them trained. Trying is not reaching: solid has reached its goal, a core in a shell is part way there or in doubt, hollow has not got there, and a faint ring is only planned.

  • Who owns new code: Has not reached it.
  • Which tests catch a break: Reached on 1 of 2.
  • Which steps carry a requirement: Has not reached it.
  • Which breaks change nothing: Reached, but doubted.
  • Which breaks will get past the tests: Reached its goal.
  • Where to add a test: Uses another goal's model.
  • A second opinion on every claim: Planned.
  • What a change will break, before the run: Planned.
  • Which methods change together: Planned.
  • Which action moves which stat: Planned, waits for 20 measured outcomes.

So far

  • Graph network reached its goal on 1 of 6 results; small model on the break's features reached its goal on 4 of 4 results (2 of them doubted) (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • 3 of 10 results change with the random seed alone, so no single run settles one (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • Giving a goal more of the graph to read helped by more than the bar in 0 of 6 tries (an anecdote: 6 results).
  • Goals where each answer belongs to about one source, in a sparse table, beat a plain rule far more often than the rest. That says where plain rules are weak, not where work is saved (right 80% of the time against a 48% base, on 44 goals across 5 graphs, and 6 of 7 on goals sealed before they ran (an anecdote at that size)).
  • No rule was found that picks the goals which save work. All 60 of the best candidates were chance or anecdote (52 goals with a measured saving, across 5 domains).
  • Ordering tests by a plain rule already saves most of what ordering them can. A learned order beat it on only 2 of 10 goals (10 goals, 31% against 33% saved).
  • The graph offers these next, relations nothing predicts yet: checked by (110 links), asserts (30 links), next step (26 links), stated by (24 links), cites (21 links).

help.head:
Help

How to use this page

Pick anything in the tree on the left and the camera flies there, with its page open down here. Pick it again, or use the bar at the top of this page, and the page closes. Flying freely leaves the page as it is.

Flying

  • Drag to orbit. Scroll or pinch to zoom. W, A, S, D fly, Q and E go down and up.
  • N and P move to the next and previous item in this part of the tree.
  • Point at a node to see what kind it is. Click or tap it to open its page: the data behind it, then what that kind of thing is. Click a slide or a reader in the world to go to it.
  • The question mark key opens this page.

The tree

  • Up and down arrows move, right opens, left closes, Enter flies. Home and End go to the ends, and typing a letter jumps to it.
  • The filter box finds anything by its words.

Links

  • Every item has its own address, so a slide or a goal can be sent as a link. Copy link is on the bar of this page.
  • A link in a page to something in the tree flies there. A link to the full manual, a concept page or the deck opens a new tab.

On a touch screen

The text of a tooltip is here, and on the page of the item you pick. A long press on a control shows it too.

  • Contents: Shows or hides the tree of everything you can fly to.
  • ‹: The tour's previous stop.
  • Tour: Start or stop the guided tour along one real thread through the graph.

sections.flatter:
Breaking code one way flatters it

A coverage tool said SemVer was 90% covered by lines run, and 85% by branches. Breaking every decision every way the tool knows made 246 breaks, 236 of them live, and 30 got past every test. 14 of those 30 sit on lines the coverage tool marks as covered.

Nothing about the code changed. Only how hard it was tried: a line that runs is not a line that is held.

That is why every pass records how wide the net was beside what got through it, and why a score from a narrow net, or from lines run, should never be trusted on its own.

On the slides: slide 2.
sections.publiccode:
On code you can read for yourself

Three trials on 30 October 2026, on code outside our own project: two parts of Unreal Engine's own C# and the scoring rules of a shipped open-source game. Every number below was measured on these runs, and every defect was reproduced by running it. No test and no product code was written for any target: only the requirements model, and /// CHECKS: comments in a scratch copy of the tests. Findings were proven with throwaway calls that are not part of any result.

What was tested

  • Unreal Engine 5.7, EpicGames.Core/SemVer.cs. Requirements: the public Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 spec, every numbered rule either mapped or excluded with a reason. Tests: EpicGames.Core.Tests, 2 of them on this class.
  • Unreal Engine 5.7, EpicGames.Core/JsonObject.cs. Requirements: the class's own doc comments, Microsoft's published Equals and GetHashCode contract, and RFC 8259. Tests: 43 on this class. 37 C# files under the engine's Source/Programs name this class.
  • osu!, a shipped rhythm game (ppy/osu, MIT, commit 845336e), ScoreProcessor.cs and HitResult.cs. Requirements: their own doc comments. Tests: the 151 test cases in osu.Game.Tests/Rulesets/Scoring. The project has many more, which this pass did not run per break: see below.

Unreal's source is available to anyone with an Unreal licence, not to the general public, so this file gives counts, method names and calls we wrote, and no engine code.

The numbers

"Live" leaves out breaks that did not compile and breaks whose compiled code was proven identical to the original.

SemVer - Coverage tool, for comparison: 90% of lines, 85% of branches. - 246 breaks made; 236 live; 206 caught (87.3%); 30 got past every test. - 14 of those 30 sit on lines the coverage tool marks as covered. - 48 of 68 statements held by a test; 18 have a break that gets past. - 7 of the 16 requirements taken from the spec have no test about them, including every rule about which strings are valid. Which test is about what was our reading of each test, written before any break ran.

JsonObject - Coverage tool: 77% of lines, 69% of branches. - 582 breaks made; 429 live; 299 caught (69.7%); 130 got past every test. - 67 of those 130 sit on lines the coverage tool marks as covered. - 176 of 289 statements held by a test; 82 have a break that gets past. - 6 questions only the class's owner can answer.

osu! scoring - Coverage tool, from those 151 tests: 72% of lines, 78% of branches. - 563 breaks made; 536 live; 286 caught (53.4%); 250 got past those 151 tests. - 145 of those 250 sit on lines the coverage tool marks as covered. - 81 of 191 statements held by those tests; 110 have a break that gets past. - Read 53.4% as what those three test files hold, and as low for the game as a whole. We applied 7 of the surviving breaks by hand and ran the rest of osu.Game.Tests: TestFailScore, TestResetFromReplayFrame and AccuracyRankAndTotalScoreOfLazerScorePreserved catch some of them. We could not finish that project on this machine: its test host crashed on the clean copy and the broken one, at different points, with and without the visual tests, so what the rest of it would catch is unknown. - This pass ran before property bodies were walked, so 5 statements in property bodies got no break.

Checking the tool's verdicts without the tool

We applied breaks the tool said no test notices, by hand, to clean copies, and ran the tests ourselves.

  • SemVer: 6 breaks at once (including CompareTo always answering "equal" and TryParse no longer testing the match): all 90 tests that run still pass, 1 is skipped. No other test project names the class.
  • JsonObject: 8 breaks, each alone, against both test projects that name the class. 7 pass everywhere: RemoveField removes nothing, Equals answers true for anything, GetHashCode is always zero, the file reader stops skipping a byte order mark, the file reader stops skipping comments, Parse refuses trailing commas, a missing double field answers true.
  • The 8th is the tests' credit. JSON false reading as true passes the class's own project, but UnrealBuildTool.Tests catches it. We had first read that as uncaught, and running the second project corrected us.
  • 8 of UnrealBuildTool.Tests' 116 tests fail on the clean copy in our setup, so they could catch nothing here.

What it found

Each of these fails when run, on the code as shipped.

SemVer against the spec - Compare throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException on valid versions, including the spec's own example compared with itself: v = SemVer.Parse("1.0.0-x-y-z.--"); v.CompareTo(v);. Any pre-release ending in a hyphen does the same. - A hyphen is treated as a separator, but the spec separates identifiers only at dots. 1.0.0-alpha-10 sorts above 1.0.0-alpha-9 (the spec says below). 1.0.0-2 sorts above 1.0.0-1-2 (below). - 1.0.0-a.b and 1.0.0-a-b compare as equal while Equals says they differ. - It accepts strings the spec rules out: "1.0.0\n", and non-ASCII digits such as an Arabic-Indic zero in 1٠.0.0. Both come from .NET's meaning of $ and \d in the spec's regular expression. - Reach: no other C# file under the install's Source/Programs or Plugins names this class, so nothing in that tree is hurt today.

JsonObject against Microsoft's contract - Equals throws NullReferenceException on any object with a null field, even x.Equals(x). The contract says it must not throw, and that x.Equals(x) is true. - Two objects that compare equal have different hash codes, which the contract forbids. A HashSet of two equal objects holds 2. We found no HashSet<JsonObject> or Dictionary<JsonObject, ...> in the engine's C#.

osu! against its doc comments - TotalScoreWithoutMods reads 1,000,000 right after ApplyBeatmap, while TotalScore reads 0, and PopulateScore before the first hit copies that 1,000,000 into the score. The field's doc says "The total number of points awarded for the score without including mod multipliers", and Reset's doc says "Resets this ScoreProcessor to a default state", but Reset never clears it. We did not trace what the game does with the value afterwards. - After a second ApplyBeatmap on one processor, MinimumAccuracy reads 1 before any hit. We did not check whether the game ever applies a beatmap twice.

JsonObject: the owner's questions, not defects we can call - Equals answers false for two parses of the same text when it holds an array or an object. - A repeated name keeps the last value at the top level and throws one level down. {"A":1,"a":2} silently keeps one field, and throws one level down. RFC 8259 only says duplicates are unpredictable between programs. - Read accepts comments and Parse refuses them. A root that is not an object throws InvalidOperationException from Read and JsonException from Parse. - {"a":1e999} parses, then ToJsonString throws. {"id":9007199254740993} writes back as ...992, which RFC 8259 allows. - TryGetIntegerField accepts the string "12". TryGetEnumField<DayOfWeek> accepts "99". On a German machine TryGetDoubleField reads the string "1.5" as 15.

What it found nothing on

  • SemVer: 13 valid strings taken from the spec, 15 of the 19 invalid strings we tried, the printed precedence chain, and build metadata were all correct. All 21 breaks of GetField and all 6 of CompareNumericFields were caught.
  • JsonObject: ToSystemJsonObject (8 of 8 caught), ToJsonNode (10 of 10), Read (5 of 5), ContainsField (3 of 3). A 562 KB file with long escaped strings read correctly, and from that we judged the pooled buffer in Read latent. That was wrong, and the control run below proved it: "all breaks of Read caught" did not mean Read was right.
  • osu!: all 41 breaks of the nine HitResult questions the tests ask about (IsHit, IsBonus, AffectsCombo and the like) were caught, and so were all 8 of ApplyBeatmap, all 11 of updateScoreMultiplier and all 5 of GetComboScoreChange. By hand, a reverted hit put the score, combo and accuracy back, and each rank's cutoff gave that rank.

Who found what

Be accurate about this. The defects above were found by an agent reading the code against each rule while writing the model: the requirements step. The breaks did not find them. The breaks measured how much the tests hold, and showed where no test looks: 9 breaks of JsonObject.Equals got past every test, and that is where the crash was. No graph neural network (GNN) played a part in any finding here.

The control run: the loop against careful reading

The trials above could not say whether the loop beats reading the code carefully, so we ran that comparison on the two Unreal classes.

Each class got two agents on the same model with the same brief, in sandboxes of their own holding a copy of the class, its tests and its contract: one with the closed loop and told to use it, one without. A scan of their transcripts found neither had read our findings above. Every claimed defect had to come with a C# program, and our harness compiled and ran each one, so nothing rests on an agent's word: none failed to compile and none hung. Three graders per class then read both reports with the arms' names hidden, beside what the harness printed.

SemVer - Without the loop: 21.9 minutes, 294,903 tokens. With it: 36.3 minutes, 414,499 tokens. - Real faults: the graders counted 4 or 5 distinct ones depending on how they grouped them, the same ones in both arms. No grader found a real fault in only one arm. - Questions for the owner: 6 without, 7 with. Wrong claims: none. - Better report: tie, tie, and one slightly for the loop, which traced each fault to its cause and line more closely.

JsonObject - Without the loop: 31.4 minutes, 389,792 tokens. With it: 33.0 minutes, 480,628 tokens. - Real faults: 11, 12 or 14 distinct ones depending on the grader, the same ones in both arms. No grader found a real fault in only one arm. - Questions for the owner: 17 to 19 without, 23 to 25 with. Wrong claims: none. - Better report: tie, tie, and one for the arm without the loop. All three graders found that the arm with the loop called more undecided things defects: 6 to 8 of them against 2 to 4.

What this says. On finding defects in a class that has a written contract, the loop added no defect, and it cost more: 1.4 times the tokens and 1.7 times the minutes on SemVer, 1.2 times the tokens on JsonObject. An agent reading carefully, with no tool of ours, found everything the loop arm found. It also found far more than our own first pass above, which spent most of its budget on the tool's bugs.

What it does not say. This is one run per class, on one model, so it is a sign and not a measure. It tested finding defects. It did not test how much the tests hold, which is what breaks are for: neither agent was asked for that number, and a reader cannot get it by reading. The loop arm's extra questions rest partly on breaks no test caught, and the graders split on what those are worth.

Faults the control run found that we had missed, each proven by the harness on the code as shipped: - Read and TryRead parse a file over 128 KiB from a pooled buffer they have already returned. A valid 173 KB file with a very long name came back with other fields silently replaced, while Parse of the same text read it correctly, and a second file made Read throw FormatException. - Name matching uses a culture comparer, so names that are different strings can count as one field. - RemoveField and AddOrSetFieldValue ignore the empty name, which RFC 8259 allows. - NaN and infinity can be set, and then ToJsonString cannot write them. An object parsed 64 levels deep cannot be written either: it reports a cycle that is not there. - TryGetEnumField throws on a struct that is not an enum. - CreateDeepCopy shares reference values it does not know how to copy, and throws on keys that differ by case and on a multi-dimensional array.

What went badly

The trial's biggest finding was in our own tool. Real code broke it five ways on the first attempts, and a sixth way on osu!, none of which our own examples had shown:

  • It silently skipped code. Any method with overloads, any operator, any generic method with a where clause and any property body was left out, and the report still read as if the whole file was held. On SemVer it saw 35 of 68 statements, missing the private Compare that does all the comparing. On JsonObject it saw 213 of 288.
  • It crashed on read-only files, which is how a Perforce workspace keeps them, on the first run.
  • It mistook a nested type's constructor for a method, and stopped.
  • One mutant with broken braces stopped the whole run.
  • An endless loop in a mutant tested alone hung the run: 11 minutes on one test host before we killed it.

It also could not read MSTest or xUnit tests' /// CHECKS: lines, only NUnit's, and it took a parameterized test's arguments for part of its name, so it reported named tests as never run. Because that fix came after osu!'s pass, its per-requirement check results are not quoted here. All of these are fixed, each with a planted test. A field's value and an indexer are still not walked, and the report now names them.

Our earlier figures on a game feature of ours came through nearly unchanged, because that code has no overloads: no existing verdict changed, and its 7 new breaks found one real gap, which a test now closes.

The budget did not hold. We set 45 minutes and 150K tokens per trial and spent about 100 minutes and over 260K output tokens, most of it on the tool's own bugs. A full pass took 13 minutes on SemVer, 9 on JsonObject and 74 on osu! (each constructor break rebuilds the game), at low priority on a busy machine. The earlier-budgeted 60 minutes for osu! did not hold either.

Re-running it

The models are in t7/ beside this file. For the Unreal trials, copy EpicGames.Core, EpicGames.Core.Tests and their props files from your own engine to a scratch folder and run closed_loop.py on the model; numbers may differ on another engine version, and these are from 5.7. For osu!, clone ppy/osu at commit 845336e, keep the three test files under osu.Game.Tests/Rulesets/Scoring, and run it the same way.
sections.accuracy:
The key is accuracy

Accuracy boosts productivity across the board. In our view it makes AI, in some cases, thousands of times smarter. That multiplier is our view, not a measurement: no multiplier of that size has been measured.

The gap between what AI guesses and what is true is what people deem AI slop. At TNT Tools the standard is no slop: every value is either read from a source, with a note of where, or marked absent with the reason. There is no third kind.

Where these numbers come from: our knowledge graph, on facts

Measured 99.03% of 35,951 derivations it had never seen were right, using reasoning rules guarded by type, on a verified-or-abstain knowledge graph of 60.33 million facts, each carrying which sources state it.

Measured 616 of 616 of its top-tier facts were right against an outside truth (cached Wikidata), on a frozen test population of 2,714 entities, with the bars declared before the run.

Measured 99.2% right on 209 held-out questions, answering 61% of them and abstaining on the rest. Asked the same questions on the same facts, a local language model answered 95% at 98.0%, with 4 confident wrong answers. The accuracy comes from being allowed to say "I don't know".

Those are facts, not code. On code, the numbers are in three trials on code you can read for yourself and six kinds of task, and the target for agents writing code with the loop is still a target. Graders on those tasks counted 17 invented values with the loop and 5 without, so "no guesses" is the standard being worked toward there, and the count is how we know.
sections.waterfall:
Back to 1999: requirements first

This is how we review our code: we pour the effort into requirements first. It is time to learn systems analysis and design again. Agile is, for the most part, dead. Long live waterfall.

The reason is mechanical. The more requirements you have, the more of the loop closes, so that nothing is left to a guess. That is what gets you slopless code. We want hand-crafted quality on an IKEA budget.

Where this comes from

Measured On Unreal Engine’s SemVer parser the requirements were written first, from the public Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 spec: 16 requirements, every numbered rule mapped to one or excluded with a reason. Writing them against the code found 4 faults that fail when run, before any break was made, and 7 of the 16 have no test about them. See on code you can read for yourself. A control run showed that an agent reading the code carefully, with no tool of ours, finds the same faults, so what pays is the requirements and the reading; the breaks add the count of what no test holds.
sections.extract:
It extracts new requirements from the ones you have

The tool automatically extracts requirements from existing requirements. You do not list them by hand. It walks each use case step by step: every step needs something to be true, and when no requirement provides that, the chain has inferred one nobody wrote. It is marked inferred and goes to the owner as a question, because only the owner can decide it. See testing raw for what that found on SemVer, and growing a model from a small seed for how far it went from 3 requirements.

Complete in, accurate out

The more complete the requirements, the more accurate the prompt built from them: an agent acting on them has less to guess. Which ones you write first matters as well, so start with the ones that run through the most code (seed it first).

Where two features meet

A large new feature often joins features you already have. We expected the walk to find the gaps where two such features meet, because each side’s requirements are already tested. We tried it once, on two features of our own game, and it does not: joined, the walk asked no new question, and an agent reading both models named places the graph missed and found real faults neither model states. No count is given because the pair is not public.

Why the graph misses them: only sets and branches make an edge to a name, so two requirements that call or read the same thing do not meet, and neither model says what it offers the other. It would take three things, none of them built: calls and reads as edges, each model declaring what it offers and what it takes, and a check that compares the two lists.

Open One pair, and not blind: the second feature was built as a clone of the first, both documents name code classes, and the agent had read one model first, so the reading number is an upper bound. Whether to remix rather than invent was not measured, and remixing with zero errors was not shown. That more complete requirements give more accurate prompts is our judgment from building with it; no run has measured it directly.
sections.firstclass:
There is no such thing as "we don't use AI"

AI is a first-class testing tool first, and a code writer second. Write every line by hand if you like: it will still tell you which of your tests cannot fail, and which code no test notices. When it does write code, it is held to the same requirements and the same tests as everyone else.

There is no reason to throw away really well done tests. That is the baby with the bathwater. Your tests become the judge of what AI does.
sections.pass:
One pass, end to end

  1. The model is read and checked against its 19 rules.
  2. The code is broken: every statement the requirements cover, every way the tool knows, all built at once.
  3. The tests run against each break separately. Each break should make some test fail.
  4. Everything goes into the graph: requirements, steps, code places, breaks, tests, and which test caught which break.
  5. The 18 checks read the graph. Each one is named after a mistake it stops.
  6. The verdict is either HOLDS, or OPEN with a list of questions and whose each one is.

You close your questions and run again. That repeat is the loop.

On the slides: slide 8.
sections.equivalents:
Breaks that change nothing

Some breaks get past every test because they do not change what the program does. Example from the kit’s own example: in Store.Buy a line with none left is already refused two statements earlier, so changing > 0 to >= 0 changes nothing the program can do. No test can catch that, and none should. These are called equivalent breaks.

The danger is calling a real missing test “equivalent” to make it go away. So the loop accepts an equivalent in only two ways:

  • Proven by the compiled code. C# compiles to IL, the instructions the runtime actually runs. If the broken copy’s IL is identical to the original’s, the two are the same program (a technique called Trivial Compiler Equivalence, Papadakis and others, 2015). The loop checks this itself.
  • Declared with a reason. Otherwise a person or agent writes down why it changes nothing, and names the methods the reason depends on. If those methods change later, the reason lapses and the break is counted as a hole again.

And if a test ever does catch a break that was declared equivalent, the declaration was wrong, and that is reported as a hole. This has happened: breaks that looked harmless could change the result, and both are now held by tests instead.

On the slides: slide 9.
sections.nodegraph:
The node graph, and flying through it

Everything the loop knows about a feature is one graph: who asked for what, which code does it, every way that code was broken, and which test noticed. The graph of osu!’s scoring rules has 1,062 nodes and 5,675 edges, SemVer’s has 448 and 1,554, JsonObject’s 1,091 and 3,840. Each is stored as SQLite and N-Triples. The fly-through of osu!’s graph draws such a store as it is, with nothing added and nothing left out. The pictures behind the slides are stills from the same page, of osu!’s scoring rules.

How it is laid out

The store has no shape of its own, so the demo gives it one you can read from top to bottom, one ring for each kind of node. On osu!’s scoring rules:

  • Why it exists: 1 source (the code’s own doc comments), 30 requirements (all written by hand, none inferred), 1 owner’s question, 5 use cases (one epic and four under it) and their 17 steps.
  • Claude’s reasoning: a chain and its steps, each citing what it stands on. This trial wrote no chain, so the ring is empty; argument chains has one, run on the kit’s example.
  • What the code does: 34 methods in a ring, sorted by name, so a class’s methods sit together.
  • What proves it: 200 branch cells (191 branches and 9 for what a judgement moves), 563 breaks and 168 tests, of which 151 ran. Each branch and each break sits at the angle of the method it belongs to, so a method and everything under it line up.

How code maps to requirements

Two kinds of edge do it. A branch maps to a requirement: 339 of those. A branch is at a method: 191. Together they take you from any decision in the code to who asked for it, and from a requirement to all the code that answers to it. A decision no requirement owns is a hole, and the loop lists it.

What the red points are

The 277 breaks no test caught. Red is what the graph records, not a verdict: 250 got past every test that ran, 13 are proven by compiled code to be the same program and 14 did not run. The 250 are the real work: none has a written reason. That is what the 53.4% means: 286 caught of the 536 live breaks, leaving out the 13 and the 14. It is what three test files hold, not what the game’s whole test project holds.

The demo

Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, W A S D to fly, Q and E for down and up. The tour follows one real thread: a source, a requirement, the step that needs it, Claude’s reasoning, the code, a branch, a break of that branch, the test that caught it, and a break that got past. The Show menu narrows it to one question: how code maps to requirements, every break and what caught it, Claude’s reasoning, requirements and use cases, or what the graph neural network reads.

It is a tool in the kit, for any graph the loop has written. --hide keeps names you choose off the page:

python graph_flythrough.py <store.sqlite> --out page.html --hide "NameA|NameB"
sections.graph:
The knowledge graph

A graph here is just a list of things (nodes) and the links between them (edges). The things are requirements, use case steps, places in the code, branches, breaks, tests and reasoning steps. The links say how they relate, for example:

requirement W-1   is checked by   test Pay_TakesExactlyThePrice
break #312        was caught by   test Pay_TakesExactlyThePrice
method Pay        is claimed by   requirement W-1

The graph is the record: the 18 checks read it, and a later agent reads it instead of re-deriving what an earlier one found. It is written on every run as a SQLite database and as an N-Triples text file, a standard format any graph tool can open.

How big it gets

Measured The graph of osu!’s scoring rules holds 1,062 nodes and 5,675 edges, SemVer’s 448 and 1,554 and JsonObject’s 1,091 and 3,840, each read from its run’s line in the morph log.

The documents are nodes too. When a number or a behaviour changes, something has to say which documents go stale, so a model can declare its documents and each section, slide and page becomes a node. A link from a requirement, stat, goal or method to a document exists only when the document names it literally, or an authored line says so and quotes the words it stands on. Likeness never makes a link. doc_nodes.py what-to-update <node> answers which documents describe a node. A document naming a requirement the model does not hold is a hole. A requirement no document describes is counted and named, not failed, because most models have never declared any documents.

On the slides: slide 11, slide 11.
sections.chains:
Argument chains: holding the agent’s explanation to the requirements

Breaking the code checks the code. A chain checks the agent’s explanation of the code. When an agent finishes a change, it writes down, step by step, why the change does what the requirements ask: each step is one claim in plain words, plus what that claim stands on. The loop then checks every step against the requirements, the code and the graph.

A chain is a written argument the agent produces on purpose, like showing your work. It is not a recording of the model’s private thinking, and the tool does not try to extract that.

What a chain looks like

A real one, run on a copy of the kit’s example, a store’s wallet. It names the question it set out to answer, then its steps; each step says one thing and cites what it stands on: a requirement’s id, a question put to the owner, or a method in the code.

chain:
  id: CH-EXAMPLE
  question: "Does a purchase stop when the stock is gone?"
  steps:
    - says: "A limited line sells its quantity and is then sold out"
      cites: [W-3, Store.Buy]

The four checks

  1. Grounded. Every cite must exist: a requirement in the model, a question the owner was asked, or a method the code really has. A step that cites nothing, or cites something that is not there, fails the run.
  2. Same words. The step’s words should share at least one word with what it cites. If they share none, the step is flagged for a person (“a new finding, or a mistake”). This is a hint, not a failure.
  3. Joined in the graph. For every pair of things one step cites, the graph must already connect them within four links. The shortcuts that would make everything look connected are not counted: the chain’s own links, the shared “space” node, and the records of breaks and tests. A pair the graph does not join is either a link the model is missing or a mistake in the argument, and a person decides which.
  4. Blind spots. Every inferred requirement (an owner’s open question) that no step cites is listed: the chain never looked there.

The chain also becomes part of the graph: a node for the chain, a node for each step, and a link from each step to everything it cites. A later agent can see which explanations rest on which requirements.

How a chain meets the code

The chain does not sit beside the graph: it goes in. Take that step, “A limited line sells its quantity and is then sold out”, citing W-3 and Store.Buy. The step becomes a node with an edge to each of those, and both were already nodes. Then the graph walks from one to the other. Here a branch of that method maps to W-3, so the two are 2 links apart, and the report says so: “grounded; the graph joins every pair it cites”. The picture on the slide is this step’s walk through the example’s graph, on down through the code, a branch, a break of that branch and the test that caught it.

Run end to end on 30 October, on a copy of the kit's example

Measured A chain with real cites: exit 0, and the chain and its step are in the graph with their cites. The same step citing a requirement that does not exist: exit 1. Citing a method the code does not have: exit 1. Citing nothing: exit 1.

Run on the kit’s example, 30 October

Measured CH-EXAMPLE: 1 step, grounded, and the pair it cites already joined in the graph, 2 links apart. The owner’s one open question, W-4 (what a refused purchase does to the stock), is a blind spot: the chain never looked at it. The whole loop on that copy held.

Across the on-against-off runs

Measured 9 chains, 102 steps: every cite resolved by the end. The checks did bite on the way there: 4 steps the graph would not join. One agent split its 2; another reported its 2 as resting only on its reading of view code no test runs. Selftests plant a step citing nothing and a cite that names nothing, and each must fail.

This is how we go after hallucination. A claim that stands on nothing cannot pass. It checks what a claim stands on, not whether it is true: a step can cite real things and still be wrong, which is why the breaks and the tests sit underneath it. So it removes the hallucination that invents a source, and cannot promise to remove all of it.

What it does not check yet

Open Whether a claim is true of the code. A real step, in one of our own runs, said “or” where the code needs both, and passed. A fresh reviewer found it. The fix being built: a step can carry a precise claim in the same form a requirement’s effect uses (for example, which two values a method branches on), and the code check tests it the way it tests an effect.

Open Whether the code a step stands on is tested. Next: a chain is accepted only if no break that got past the tests sits in code one of its steps stands on.

On the slides: slide 12, slide 12.
sections.map:
The requirements map to the code, and the map finds mistakes

This is an early prototype. Every requirement links to the code it owns, in one graph. The graph's criteria and the breaks do most of the finding so far. A graph neural network (GNN) learns on the same map, proposes which requirement owns new code, and is set to learn what does not fit; using it as a second opinion on every claim is planned and not yet measured.

What the map has found

Measured 7 of the 16 requirements taken from the SemVer spec have no test about them, including every rule about which strings are valid. Which test is about what was our reading of each test, written down before any break ran.

Measured 110 of the 191 branches of osu!’s scoring rules have a break that got past the three test files that were run, and every one of the 191 is claimed by a requirement, so those 110 are tests missing, not requirements missing. Read it as what those three files hold.

Measured On public code: a public asteroid game's document modelled as 48 requirements. 10 rest on a function's behaviour with no value behind them, and the parse check caught a document row missing a column. Language-neutral parts only, with no breaks, since there is no JavaScript adapter; a thin graph, where a green result means little.

Measured On the toolkit's own code: 885 of the 1,532 breaks caught. See the tool on itself.

Open That trial is done, on C#: see code you can read yourself. There is no C++ adapter, so on C++ it would run the language-neutral parts only.
sections.gnnhow:
How the GNN works, what it records, and how it tries to improve

How it works

  1. It reads. Each node starts as its own words, hashed to 512 numbers.
  2. It listens. GraphSAGE layers let each node hear its neighbours, relation by relation. After that a node's numbers say something about what surrounds it.
  3. It ranks. A scorer ranks every requirement for a decision that has no owner.
  4. It asks. Below 70% sure it abstains. Above that, its answer goes out as a question for a person or an exact check. It is never a verdict.

It never reads breaks, tests or chains. Those hold the answer, and new code would not have them. Two ways that answer leaked in were measured and closed before any score here was taken. Whole methods are held out when it is tested, so each score is on code it has not seen.

What it records

  • Its score beside the plain rules, on each pass run with --gnn (stats.jsonl): the GNN, the best plain rule, the words alone, random and the same method, in mean reciprocal rank, where 1.0 is always ranked first.
  • Each job against the best plain rule (kg/gnn_tasks.jsonl): who owns new code, which tests catch a break, which steps carry a requirement, which breaks are the same program. The results.
  • The shape of what it reads: its nodes and links, how many are owner links, how many methods, and how those links pile up: how few requirements hold most of them.
  • Breaks ranked (kg/survivor_rank.jsonl): how many of the survivors a learned order finds in the first fifth of a run, on average over ten seeds, against the plain rule and random. One seed flatters, so only the mean over seeds is recorded.
  • Its curve (gnn_curve): its score by how much of the links it can see.
  • How sure it was: at 70% sure or more, how often it was right and on how much of the new code, by seed.
  • Every tune (gnn_tune.jsonl): each variant's score, and what was kept.

How it tries to improve

Its lead over the plain rules is itself a stat. When that lead falls as more tests arrive, the telemetry reports it as worsening and names reshaping the graph as a next job, beside writing tests. A tune is due after 5 passes without one anyway. A standing tick or a person then runs it: graph_gnn.py tune <graph>. A tune redraws what the GNN reads, with each relation left out and each derived link added. A change is kept only if it wins by 0.02 on the tuning seeds and again on a seed it was not chosen on.

So far

Measured Tunes have been run and nothing was kept: no variant won by the bar of 0.02. It attempts to improve itself, and the attempt has not paid yet.

Open A project's run plan records whether each learned job wins there. 3 of its 7 lines reach what a pass runs, wired by the tool's own tick, and all 3 are off today because a plain rule wins. The other 4 are measured only.
sections.gnn:
The GNN: who owns new code?

When someone adds code, the loop needs to know which requirement it belongs to. The GNN (a graph neural network, a learning model that reads the graph) suggests an answer. It looks at what is already linked around that code and ranks the requirements from most to least likely owner.

How it was tested fairly

It was trained on part of a project’s graph, with whole methods hidden from it. Then it was asked to rank owners for the hidden methods, code it had never seen. It was compared against simple rankers that do not learn, such as “the requirements already linked to this method” or “the requirement whose words overlap the code’s names most”. It is only allowed to make suggestions if it beats them.

What the numbers mean

MRR (mean reciprocal rank) scores a ranking: the right owner ranked first scores 1, second scores ½, third ⅓, and so on, averaged over every test case. An MRR of 0.75 means the right owner is usually first, sometimes second.

Where these numbers come from

Measured On the tool’s own code, with whole methods held out and a mean over five seeds, the GNN scored MRR 0.65 against 0.72 for the best ranker that does not learn: it loses, and is switched off there. Runs differ by about a tenth, so a single number is never the whole story.

Measured It only wins on a large enough graph that is about half claimed: see Seed it first, then it flies.

Measured The design is to abstain: below 70% sure the GNN says “not sure” and asks. How often it is right at 70% and on how much of the new code was measured on one project of ours, and is not repeated here because that project is not public.

Its suggestions are always questions for a person, never verdicts. One lesson from building it: the first version did worse than the simple rankers, because the links it was asked to predict were also links it could read. Separating the two fixed it.

On the slides: slide 3, slide 16.
sections.gnnself:
The tool on its own networks

The requirements for each learned part are a subgraph of their own: one use-case model per part, with the stats it reads and records as a closed list inside it, all joined in one graph of 3,283 nodes and 7,987 edges, where 30 stats are shared across parts. The loop then ran on each part, breaking its code, and each part was run on a graph of itself.

What it measured, on 30 October

Measured No part beat the plain rules on its own code. Who owns new code: 0.75 against 0.83. Which tests catch a break: 0.83 against 0.92. Which steps carry a requirement: 0.66 against 0.81. Which breaks get past the tests: 0.15 against 0.19. Two were too thin to say: which breaks change nothing, and where to add a test. One seed each, so these are not means.

Measured 48 requirements, 9 of them inferred. 140 stats, used 229 times across the parts, 32 of them read by nobody. 369 breaks caught, 205 got past. 115 of the catches came only from new guards written from the requirements, because the tool's own selftests had passed those breaks.

Open 1,238 of the 1,812 breaks did not run, 960 of them on the largest part, so the counts are lower bounds.

What it found, none of it fixed yet

  • With the guard that keeps the answer out of what a network reads removed, the network's own selftest still passes. Only the new guard catches it.
  • One win is probably not one: which breaks change nothing, on the tool's own code, learned from labels written before a fix to how breaks are compared. Inferred, not re-run. On both projects every example it learns from is a break a pass already removes, so its score says nothing about the survivors a person reads.
  • The bar for showing a proposal has no margin, so 0.51 against 0.50 passes, and it leaves out the plain rule that actually wins on one project.
  • The run plan reads only the last row, and the row names no seed, so two losing seeds and one winning one switch a part on.
  • The code that writes a score is not held by a test: 32 of 32 breaks of it got past.
  • The Python adapter only breaks statements inside functions, so the thresholds and the guard list themselves were never broken by it.

Running the rules on the improvement model itself, a level up, is still open.
sections.selfimprove:
Self-improvement, on by default

The tool tests itself, and that is on unless you turn it off. It happens at two sizes.

Every pass. A pass writes one row of stats about itself to the morph log, checks those stats against the tool's own requirements for improving, and prints what to improve next. Nothing about your code changes.

The standing tick. A fresh agent with no memory takes one item, measures the same stat before and after the change, and records whether it was worth it. Both ship in this kit, with the self-improving qualities we built for our ARC3 harness. Nothing starts a tick for you: TICK.md is its runbook, and you schedule it.

Turning it off

Run with --no-self-improve, or put self_improve: false in the model's loop: block. The pass then records no row and prints no picks. There may be some token saving, but on a pass it is small; the larger spend is the tick, which only runs if you schedule it, and stops when you stop scheduling it or create .loop_tick.STOP beside the tools.

Where these numbers come from

Measured A pass: 44 stats in a row, about a third of a second to collect them, three printed lines for the agent to read. On the kit's Python example, a clean install, with it off a pass wrote no row and printed 295 fewer characters.

Measured A tick: the app counted 197,134 tokens for the first tick and 291,042 for the second, over 9 and 22 minutes.

One shared graph, not networked in this version

Ideally everyone working on a project shares one graph, because it also works as a retrieval store (retrieval-augmented generation, RAG): an agent looks up what is already proven instead of re-reading the files to work it out again. We share ours across the team that way, in the belief that it saves tokens. This version is not networked, and each checkout keeps its own graph; you could add sharing in whatever way suits your network.

Where this is not measured

Open How far a shared graph cuts what an agent reads has not been measured. To learn who owns a method, what it must do and which tests catch it, the graph holds rows for that method and the files hold the model, the source and the tests; no agent has been timed using either, so a saving is a belief and not a measurement.

What it has found so far

Where these numbers come from

Measured 19 ways a check could pass for the wrong reason, found by fresh reviewers; 17 fixed, each with a planted mistake a selftest must catch (see reviewers).

Measured 11 stats were recorded with nothing reading them. The audit first said 6, and that was itself a bug: it counted test fixtures and the recorder as readers. Now 0: each stat triggers something, or has a reader with a date.

Measured 32 requirements on its own stats, 2 records banked for a learner that does not exist yet, and 4 triggers firing now. Each trigger that fires is a work item. It was 12 until a tick found that 8 of them fired on every pass whatever happened.

Measured 9 faults its first round of on against off found in itself: 5 in the harness, 4 in the tool, all fixed.

Measured Its optional parts: of the run plan's 7 lines, 3 reach what a pass runs, and on today's evidence all 3 are off on both projects, because a plain rule wins by more than the 0.02 a learned part would need. The other 4 are marked measured only: they record a verdict and change nothing, and three of the verdicts behind the plan flip with the seed alone. Its own tick found that none of the 7 reached a pass by code before it wired these.

Measured 58% of the breaks of its own code are caught, 885 of 1,532, on its one self pass. The tool is less tested than the feature it tests.

Open 0 of the 20 measured outcomes its improvement learner needs, so rules choose the work for now, not a model. These numbers show what it has found, not yet how fast it gets better.

The loop, in pseudo C++

The toolkit is written in Python. This is the same logic for a C++ reader; the lower-case names are the real ones in the code.

// One pass. Self-improvement is on by default.
Verdict run(Model& m, bool selfImprove = true) {
  Breaks  b = Mutate(m.code);       // one compile
  Results r = RunEachAlone(b, m.tests);
  Graph   g = KnowledgeGraph(m, r);
  Holes   h = Criteria(g);          // 18 checks

  if (self_improve_on(m, selfImprove)) {
    Row row = PassStats(m).collect();  // 44 stats
    MorphLog(m).add(row);
    auto fired = improvement::fires(rules, log);
    Print(NextImprovement(log, fired).picks());
  }

  return h.ours.empty() ? HOLDS : OPEN;
}

// One tick. A fresh agent, one item, no memory.
void Tick() {
  Start s = loop_tick::start();     // the lock
  if (s.stopped || s.busy || s.idle) return;
  if (s.epochStarts) Brainstorm();  // every 12
  RunSelftests();                   // red = item
  telemetry_audit();                // unread = item
  Item i = Choose(improvement::check(), board);
  Stat before = i.stat.Measure();
  i.Do();                           // one change
  Stat after = i.stat.Measure();
  if (s.epochEnds) {
    run_plan::decide();             // parts on or off
    improvement::graph();           // did it work?
  }
  loop_tick::finish(i, before, after, worth);
}

Three ticks in a row worth "no" and the tick sleeps until something it watches changes, so an idle loop costs almost nothing. The improvement graph is the same shape one level up: stats are its code, triggers its requirements, ticks its tests.
sections.recursive:
The loop on its own improvement

The loop records a great deal about itself: every pass leaves fifty numbers, and the learned parts leave evidence of when they help. Recording a number is only worth it if something reads it and acts. On 29 October an audit found 28 numbers that nothing read, and many more that were only printed.

So the improvement of the loop now has requirements of its own, written the way the product's are. Each number has a requirement saying what pattern in it should trigger something, what that is, and why the number is kept: a test that catches nothing for two passes is a speed item; an excuse for a harmless break that lapses is a hole; the graph not growing for three passes means the model is not being seeded. A number kept for a learner that does not exist yet must name that learner and a date. Past the date, unread, it fails.

Three levels, one graph

  • Level 1, the product. The loop holds the code to the product's requirements.
  • Level 2, the improvement. The loop holds itself to its improvement requirements, with the same kind of closure rules: every number covered, every trigger that fires acted on, every action naming the number it meant to move and its result measured, and an action that never moves its number retired.
  • Level 3 is level 2 again. How well the improvement graph is doing (numbers covered, triggers acted on, actions that worked) is itself written as numbers with requirements, so they sit in the same graph. The tower closes on itself.

The same learning applies one level up: once enough actions have measured results, a model can learn which kind of action moves which number, and it is switched on only where it beats the plain rule, like everything else.

Where these numbers come from

Measured The audit on 29 October: 28 numbers read by nothing at first; after giving each a reader or a trigger, none. 19 now drive a decision in code and 25 are covered by a trigger.

Measured The first run of the triggers fired 12: among them, 5 tests in the tool's own suite that catch no break at all, 8 of the who/what/why questions never asked on each model, and one requirement whose breaks were all caught last pass and are not now.

Open No action has a measured result yet; the improvement graph becomes learnable at 20.
sections.matrix:
Six kinds of task, on against off

One pair says little, so on 29 October six small tasks of different kinds were each given to two agents, one with the loop and one without. Each task has a hidden acceptance test, written before either agent started and proven first: it passes a reference solution and fails the untouched code. Beside it sits a second score, after the novelty review below: the tests each answer leaves behind are run against plausible wrong versions of the feature (a refund that forgets the stock, a menu that wraps only one way), and the score is how many of those wrong versions they catch. Each wrong version was itself checked to fail the hidden test first.

Where these numbers come from

Measured A refund (C#, precise): both passed the hidden test 7 of 7, and both left tests that catch 9 of 9 wrong versions. With the loop: 203,945 tokens and 14.5 minutes; without: 128,015 and 5.1. The blind grader preferred the answer made without the loop, which also guarded a stock count against overflow.

Measured A bulk purchase (Python, precise): both 9 of 9 on the hidden test and 9 of 9 wrong versions caught. With the loop: 237,213 tokens and 9.4 minutes; without: 128,011 and 3.2. The grader preferred the loop answer, on a point that favours the loop's own habits (it declared a harmless break the way the model already does).

Measured "Make buying fairer" (vague): without the loop the agent changed nothing and asked the owner four questions; with it, the agent added a "how much you are short" helper and a forgiveness amount that starts at zero, and wrote the amount down as the owner's question. Both pass the hidden test, which holds only the rules already stated. 214,714 tokens and 15 minutes against 103,391 and a minute. The grader preferred the loop answer; the other agent's questions were only in its reply, which the grader never sees.

Measured Owners for 13 unowned branches (the model only): both gave every method an owner. With the loop: 309,133 tokens and 47 minutes, closing 14 holes and opening one it could not close; without: 251,751 and 8 minutes. Both pass the corrected hidden test 12 of 12 (the first version of that test had two flaws of its own, both reported).

Measured A menu that wraps (Unity, a requirement an existing test contradicts): both 7 of 7. With the loop: 352,912 tokens and 77 minutes; without: 189,555 and 7. The grader preferred the loop answer: the other quietly changed an edge case the task said to keep.

Measured A bug in the tool itself: both 8 of 8. With the loop: 297,545 tokens and 145 minutes (two full passes over the tool's own code); without: 127,704 and under 3. The grader preferred the loop answer, whose tests pinned more of the behaviour. Along the way the loop arm found four real bugs in the tool, all since fixed.

The six, by their first blind grader: the loop answer was preferred 4 times, the answer without it twice. Every answer passed its hidden test either way.

The same tasks again, and three graders on each

On 30 October five of the six were repeated with the same hidden tests and the tools as they then stood. The sixth, the bug in the tool itself, could not be repeated because that bug is now fixed. One grader per pair turned out to be too noisy, so two more blind graders then judged every pair, each with its own coin for which answer is X, on briefs with the arm's tells removed.

Where these numbers come from

Measured By the majority of three graders: the loop preferred on 7 of 11 pairs, the answer without it on 3, 1 split. Round 1: loop 5, without 1. Round 2: loop 2, without 2, 1 split. All three graders agreed on 7 of the 11.

Measured What one grader would have told you. With only the first grader, rounds 1 and 2 together came to 5, 5 and 1, and 3 of the 5 repeated tasks reversed. With three graders, 1 reversed (the fairer rule) and 1 went to a split (the wrapping menu). The noise was the single grader.

Measured The losses are consistent. The model-only task went against the loop 3 to 0 in both rounds. On the fairer rule's repeat, 3 to 0 against: the loop arm removed a public constructor, so the hidden test no longer compiled, while the loop reported that everything held. The loop does not yet hold the public surface of the code (a planned check).

Measured What the 28 newer grades counted (6 of them compare the loop to the hint arm below): left unfinished, 9 with the loop and 18 without; scope creep, 4 and 10; invented values, 17 and 5. The loop writes more down, and graders call some of that invented.

Measured Two first grades are weaker than the rest. Three loop arms of the 27 read the run's own notes, which can say how the other arm finished, and two diffs named the arm or the tool. Those tells are now blanked for graders and each arm can be scanned for what it read. The first grade of each pair is still on the older brief.

A cheap hint instead of the loop

A third kind of arm got no loop at all, only a short list before writing its tests: the statements of the code it changed most likely to let a break past the tests, learned from the project's own past results.

Where these numbers come from

Measured Three tasks against the loop arm. Every answer passed its hidden test. Tests left behind were equal on all three (9 of 9, 9 of 9, 7 of 8). The bulk purchase tied. On the refund and the wrapping menu the grader preferred the loop answer, but the code behaved the same and the edge was in what it wrote down, such as recording the new rule as a requirement. The loop arm cost 1.7 to 2.3 times the tokens and 3 to 10 times the minutes of the hint arm.

Growing a model from a small seed

What looked like the largest gap went away once the run was fair. An agent was given a feature's problem story, its sources and its 3 most cross-cutting requirements, and asked to grow the rest of the model; another did the same without the loop. Each was scored by how many of the real model's other requirements it arrived at, matched by the methods they own, never by wording.

Where these numbers come from

Measured With the requirement ids removed from the code: 16 of 24 each, a tie. Of the requirements each grew, 14 of 46 matched a real one with the loop and 12 of 41 without. With the loop: 511,317 tokens and 81 minutes; without: 323,773 and 17. One run each, and neither arm asked for anything it should not see.

Measured The first run read 19 of 24 against 10, at 515,241 tokens and 68 minutes against 277,720 and 13, but the code cited its requirement ids, so both arms started with more than the 3. Do not quote it. Recovering a model is not where the loop has shown a gain.

What it says so far. On small tasks correctness does not separate the two: nearly every answer passed its hidden test, and the tests left behind were as strong either way where they could be compared. Graders still prefer the loop's answers more often than not, mostly for what they leave finished and written down. The loop cost 1.2 to 2.3 times the tokens and 3 to 55 times the time. Where it does differ is in what gets written down: the open questions, the new requirement, the reason a claim changed. That fits when it fits: the loop is meant to pay over many changes, and that has not been measured yet. Inside one small change it does not, and the one fair test of building a model tied.

The harness was tested too. Five of its own faults turned up and were fixed: hiding a chain's file name blanked a plain word in one answer and voided a grade; the grader was told the requirements were those of one feature for every task; one hidden test was stricter than its task; answers given only in a reply are invisible to the grader; and the loop brief told a model-only task to write tests.

The first round's two losses still say something, whichever way the repeats went. On the refund the answer without the loop guarded an overflow the loop answer missed. On the model-only task the loop answer closed its holes by pinning code on requirements whose words do not cover it: the count of holes reached zero without the intent being met. That is now a planned check (a second opinion on every claim).

Open Three graders per pair with their agreement counted, so a verdict only counts where they agree; arms that cannot reach the other arm's files and diffs that cannot name their arm; the grown model repeated on code that cites no ids; and the tests-left-behind score made fair for tests that also check a choice of their own.
sections.landscape:
Where it stands among the other tools

We set out to find every agent requirements tool we could, rank them, rank this kit beside them by the same rubric, and take the abilities they have that it lacks. The danger in a comparison like this is a rubric built from what one's own tool happens to do, which proves nothing. So the rubric was committed first, before any tool was scored, with its weights, its predictions and the checks on the order.

It has 17 criteria in two groups. Ten are what other tools are good at and this kit may not be: asking a person good questions, gathering from conversation or documents, ease of first use, install friction, editor and agent integration, working on an existing codebase, a team's review workflow, adoption, price and licence. Seven are what the loop was built for: finding holes in the requirements, tying them to code, tying them to tests, proving a test catches a break, checking the agent's argument for a change, keeping requirements true over time, and measured evidence that it works. Each criterion says how a score from 0 to 3 is earned and what evidence counts. Two weightings were fixed before scoring: every criterion once, and the nine a typical team names first (a judgement, not a survey).

Every score carries one kind of evidence. READ is the tool's own page, with its link. TRIED is something we ran, which only our own kit can have, since nothing of anyone else's was installed. ABSENT is a search of named pages that found nothing: a search result and not a proof, worth 0. SECOND_HAND is a third party, or a search summary of a page we did not fetch, and is capped at 2. CLAIM is a tool's own marketing with no measurement behind it, capped at 1, because a claim is not a measurement. A check, landscape.py --check, refuses a score with no page behind it, a tool with no link and a criterion nobody scored, and its selftest plants each refusal and sees it fire.

Measured Read on 2026-10-30: 31 tools, 28 of them ranked beside the kit, all 31 read at their own pages and 15 with released code. 493 scores: 258 read at the tool's own page, 213 not found on the pages read, 13 second-hand, 7 marketing claims, 2 run by us.

Measured With all 17 criteria counting once the kit scores 70.6 of a possible 100 and is 1st; next is Rebuild Dossier at 60.8. On the 9 criteria a team names first it scores 48.1 and is 10th, tied with Devin; OpenSpec leads at 70.4. On the deep criteria alone it scores 95.2 and is 1st; Rebuild Dossier is next at 61.9.

Open Our place depends on the weights: yes. Over 10,000 random weightings the kit is in the top third in 99.9% and first in 90.0%, median place 1, range 1 to 13. Leaving out any one criterion leaves it 1st. Granting every absence on a deep criterion one point, or counting no marketing claim, leaves its place unchanged. Scoring ourselves one point lower on every deep criterion gives 2nd at equal weights; one point lower on every score gives 8th at equal weights and 22nd on the team list.

sections.limits:
What it is not, yet

The first trial on code anyone can read

Measured The C# adapter was skipping code without saying so. On Unreal's own SemVer.cs it saw 35 of 68 statements, including none of the private method that does all the comparing, and on JsonObject.cs 213 of 288. It dropped overloaded methods, operators and generic methods with a where clause, and does not walk property bodies. The report still read as if the whole file was held. An earlier target of ours has no overloads, which is why its numbers never showed it.

Open All fixed, each with a planted case: naming every overload and operator, a report that names what it did not walk, a read-only tree such as a Perforce workspace, a constructor of a nested type, one bad break stopping a whole run, and a break that hangs a test forever. A field's value and an indexer are still not walked, and the report says so. Re-running that target changed no verdict.

  • A prototype. Version 0.1. Its own model still names holes.
  • A thin model misleads. A green report over a small model reads as proof and is not (why).
  • Setup comes first. A problem story, requirements, use cases and tests a machine can run, before it helps at all.
  • Not a chatbot. It is a harness for agents that build systems. It does not answer questions.
  • It refutes, it never proves. “Closed” means closed against the breaks it tried (why).
  • Feel is not checked. Visuals, timing and feel still need a person to look.

Used where it does not fit, it can be worse than not using it at all.
