sections.lineage:
Where it comes from: a mutation of an ARC3 self-improvement loop

This toolkit is a mutation of the self-improvement loop from our ARC3 harness, which was a piece of a failed attempt at AGI. It was first built against one of our own game features, which is internal and cannot be extracted, so what is shown here is run on public code instead: Unreal Engine’s SemVer parser and JSON object, osu!’s scoring rules, and the toolkit’s own source. What came across is the part that survived: propose, then verify; abstain rather than guess; and never trust a number you could game.

What the ARC3 work measured

Measured A weak proposer and a strong verifier beat either alone. On a frozen set of 63 games, at a budget of 150 steps, the unified agent reached 31 where random reached 14. At 250 steps it reached 35 against random's 29, reproduced identically twice.

Measured The failure that shaped this tool. An autonomous self-improvement run went 16 days and 330 commits and found nothing that generalized. A counter that could be gamed rose from 147 to 168 while the honest number stayed flat. That is why here every stat must have a reader, a control and a fresh reviewer, and why the loop audits its own stats.

Measured The honest baseline. The one-shot solver covered all 249 games and reached 106 of them, but blind transfer to games it had not seen was about 1 of 81. We report that number because it is the real one.

If this harness is useful to you and working together does not happen, perhaps the harnesses can merge: it is self-improving, so a merged one keeps improving for both sides.
sections.install:
Install

Get it from github.com/rj45Thompson/closed-loop-kit, under the MIT licence.

python install.py              # install for this user
python install.py --check      # check only, copy nothing
python install.py --uninstall  # remove what it put down, nothing else

It puts the skill where Claude Code finds it and the tools beside it. It needs Python 3.10 or newer and PyYAML. PyTorch (for the GNN), the .NET SDK (for the C# adapter and the example) and PowerShell 7 (for the IL comparison) are optional; if one is missing it says what that piece would have done, and never pretends it ran.

Then it runs every selftest in the installed copy, and the whole loop on the example: a small wallet and store in C#, with NUnit tests that each name the requirement they check. The example must hold: everything closed except one question that only its owner can answer.

What a clean install showed

Measured Installing the built kit into an empty folder on 29 October: every selftest passes with PyTorch, scikit-learn and the .NET SDK (14 of 20 on Python and PyYAML alone, the rest named as skipped), and the loop over the example’s 58 breaks reported HOLDS.

sections.targets:
The two targets

These are goals for the loop at its full potential, used where it fits. Neither has been measured yet.

95% accuracy or better

Target Agents using the loop on work it fits should get the task right at least 95 times in 100. The remaining 5% would be bugs in our own code.

How it will be measured: the on/off harness, graded blind, counted per failure pile, with the hidden acceptance test deciding whether the task was done.

Up to 90% fewer tokens

Target On average, up to 90% fewer tokens per closed requirement, because a later step looks up what the graph already holds instead of re-reading and re-deriving it. This number is always being re-evaluated.

How it will be measured: the same harness, from each arm’s own usage records (the tokens the model read and wrote), per task.

Measured The first data point goes the other way: on one small, precisely specified task, the loop used 58% more tokens for the same correctness (details). The target is about larger systems held across many changes, where re-reading and re-deriving is what costs; that has not been measured yet.

What is next: from a rough epic to code that is right

The tool’s main intent is to take the requirements for a game from a rough epic use case and grow them into a larger set, so that the code written from them is as accurate as it can be. The question behind it is a question and not a result: if the requirements for something very difficult are complete and checked, how far does that move what an AI can build? The direction is better tools for making video games, not general intelligence.

Measured How much of existing code its tests hold, on three public targets, and that an agent reading carefully finds the same faults the loop does (on code you can read for yourself).

Open The epic-to-code test has not run: no rough epic has been grown into requirements, and no code written from grown requirements has been graded. The test we plan starts from one rough epic for a small game whose right answers come from an independent published source. Agents write the code with and without the grown requirements, and hidden tests written from that source, never from our model, grade both blind. Tokens per arm are recorded, with how many requirements the epic grew into and how many the hidden tests needed that it missed.

On the slides: slide 25, slide 28.
sections.questions:
Where the model asks who, what, why

Good requirements answer seven questions: who acts, what they want, why, when it starts, where it happens, what must be true before, and what is true after. The model has three levels where these can be asked: a use case, a step inside it, and an extension (what happens when a step cannot complete). Each level has a field for some of the questions and none for others.

Measured on SemVer

Measured Use cases (4): all seven answered in every one. The model’s rules require them.

Measured Steps (15): what and why answered in all 15; who, when, where, before and after are never asked, because a step has no field for them.

Measured Extensions (4): what, why, when and after answered; who, where and before never asked. That is 74 answered and 8 never asked; the 8 are the same on every model.

So the gaps are not in the summaries but one level down, in the steps between them. These counts go into the morph log every pass. Open Whether asking more at the step level makes agents more accurate, or just slower, is for the on/off pairs to measure once there are enough of them.
sections.model:
The model: your requirements as data

The model is a few small text files (YAML) beside your code:

  • The problem story: one paragraph on what the system is for, each sentence with where it came from (a person, a design document, a date).
  • Requirements, each with an id, its text, how to check it, its source, and the code it points at. A requirement is authored (someone wrote it) or inferred (the loop found that a step needs it and nobody wrote it). Inferred ones are questions for the owner, never facts.
  • Use cases: who wants what, as 3 to 11 numbered steps, plus what happens when a step cannot complete. Each step names the requirement it relies on.
  • The loop block: which code folders and test files the loop works on.

The 19 rules refuse a model that is malformed before anything runs. Some examples of what they refuse, in their own words: a use case with too few or too many steps; “step 3 carries no requirement”; “a requirement with no text”; “no measure: nothing says how to check it”; a story sentence with no source; two items sharing one id; a use case with “no alternate pathway: what happens when a step cannot complete?”; a requirement carried only by summary steps, so no real user goal ever reaches it.

On the slides: slide 8, slide 8.
sections.breaks:
Breaking the code on purpose

The usual name is mutation testing, and each broken copy is a mutant. This manual calls them breaks. A break that makes some test fail is caught (or “killed”). A break that every test still passes got past (or “survived”), and that points at a missing test.

A small example

if (wallet.Money >= price)   // the real code: exact money is enough
if (wallet.Money >  price)   // a break: paying the exact price now fails

If every test still passes with the second line, then no test buys something with exactly enough money. That is a missing test, and the report names the line.

The kinds of break the C# adapter makes, in plain words:

  • Conditions: turned around, forced always true, forced always false.
  • Operators: < made <=, == made !=, && made ||, plus made minus.
  • Values: a number made one more, true made false, a text emptied, a function argument replaced by its default.
  • Structure: the two outcomes of a ? : swapped, an else branch removed, a statement removed, the whole method made to return at once.

Each statement gets at most 24 breaks, one of each kind first, so a busy statement cannot crowd out the kinds of break that matter most.

On the slides: slide 9.
sections.owner:
The right test must notice

It is not enough that some test fails when a requirement’s code is broken. It should be that requirement’s own test. Otherwise the requirement is only protected by accident: a test written for something else happens to fail today and may not tomorrow.

So each test says what it checks, on the line above it:

/// CHECKS: W-1
[Test]
public void Pay_TakesExactlyThePrice() { ... }

A requirement whose named test misses its own breaks is a hole, even when another test caught them. And a test named as a requirement’s check that catches none of that requirement’s breaks is a hole too, so listing more tests can never make the score look better.

On the slides: slide 3, slide 21.
sections.tuner:
Shaping the graph for the GNN

The GNN learns from the graph’s links, and not every kind of link helps it. A tuning pass tries leaving out one kind of link at a time (for example the link from every branch to the one shared “space” node, which ties everything to everything) and measures the GNN again on code it never saw. A change is kept only if it helps on the tuning runs and again on a separate run it was not chosen on, so that a lucky result is not mistaken for a real one. The kept choice is written beside the graph, and the GNN reads it from then on.

The stats decide when to tune: when the GNN’s lead over the simple rankers stops growing, or every five passes otherwise (how the stats choose).

The first tune, on the graph the network was built on

Measured The full graph set the score to beat, and run-to-run noise alone was about 0.02. Six variants were tried. None beat the full graph by the required 0.02, so nothing was changed. The best, leaving out the use-case structure links, gained a little; leaving out the shared “space” node gained less.

Measured The links the GNN relied on most were “binds requirement” and “is at”, which ties a branch to its method.

The second tune: adding links, three runs each

Measured Adding links the graph lacks did not help beyond the noise: linking the methods of one class, and linking requirements one step carries together, each gained under 0.01. Leaving out the use-case structure links was the only change never worse on any run, and it stayed under the 0.02 bar. Nothing was changed.

What that says: on this graph the GNN already gets what the structure can give it. The next gains are more likely from more graphs to learn from and better descriptions of each node than from reshaping this one.
sections.ab:
On against off

The loop’s own report cannot say whether the loop helps, because it grades work by its own rules. So there is a separate harness. One task goes to two agents, each in its own copy of the code. One works with the loop (the on arm), one without it (the off arm). Neither is told it is being compared.

  1. The task is a real prompt, taken from the team’s own past sessions.
  2. The harness measures what each arm produced. It never takes an arm’s word for it.
  3. A third agent grades both answers blind: it sees the task, the two changes labelled X and Y, and the measured results, and it does not know which arm is which.
  4. Every failure goes into one pile by kind (wrong behaviour, a missed requirement, an invented value, a weak test, and so on). “Different but both fine” has its own pile, so two good answers that differ are not counted as a failure.

A hidden acceptance test, written first

An arm’s own tests only show that it agrees with itself. So from the second pair on, the person setting up the pair writes an acceptance test before either arm starts. Neither arm ever sees it. It is copied into each arm’s copy only to be measured, then removed. The harness refuses to accept the test once either arm’s copy exists, refuses it if it changed after it was set, and proves beforehand that it can fail (on the code before the change) and can pass (on a reference change kept apart from both arms). The blind grader sees that test’s result, and not the arms’ own test counts.

What happened so far

Measured The first pair: both arms passed their own tests. The on arm hit a crash in the loop itself (it failed when the code and the copy sat on different drives). That crash is fixed, and the pair counts as “tool failed”, neither for nor against the loop.

Measured The second pair, the first fair one (a small task: say what unlocks a line that is not on sale yet). The hidden test was proven first: it fails on the code before the change, on two wrong answers that compile, and passes on a reference answer kept apart from both arms.

  • Correctness: a tie. Both answers pass the hidden test 5 of 5 and their own 49 tests, and both mark the new wording as an open question for the owner.
  • Cost: the loop cost more. With the loop: 337,580 tokens and 39 minutes. Without it: 214,293 tokens and 6.5 minutes. That is 58% more tokens on this task, not fewer.
  • The blind grader preferred the answer made without the loop, because it stayed inside the task. The loop arm’s one failure was scope creep: following the loop’s report, it fixed listed items its change had not caused.

One pair is one data point, on the kind of task this manual says the loop is not for: small and precisely specified. It still showed two things to fix. The arm started in a model with hundreds of old holes it had not caused, and the report did not separate the holes its change made from those already there. Both are on the board.

The off arm still follows the project’s own working rules (never guess a value, say what was not verified), so the comparison measures the tool, not discipline.

On the slides: slide 23.
sections.raw:
The point of all of it

Testing raw: AI that tests the requirements

We test code. Requirements get reviewed by people, now and then. What AI adds is requirements testing done by a machine, all the time, at the scale of the code. This loop is built for exactly that.

The requirements are the code behind the code. When an agent writes the program, it writes it from the requirements, so in its rawest form the requirements are the code. A mistake in a requirement becomes a mistake in every line written from it. Testing before that stage, on the requirements themselves, is what we call testing raw.

It makes new requirements by finding failures in the ones it has. The loop walks each use case step by step and asks what every step needs. When a step needs something no requirement provides, that gap is a failure of the requirements, and it becomes a new requirement: marked inferred, and put to the owner as a question.

Measured

Measured On SemVer the model holds 16 requirements taken from the spec and 3 marked inferred: what the spec leaves unsaid and the class needs, each put to the owner as a question, for example “Parse throws on exactly the strings TryParse refuses”. On osu!’s scoring rules all 30 were written from the code’s own doc comments and none was inferred.

Open How many requirements a rough epic grows into, and whether code written from them is more accurate, has not been measured: see the two targets.

The code still gets tested. Breaking the code on purpose (how) is how the loop checks that each requirement really reached the code. But the requirements are tested first, because that is where a mistake is cheapest to catch.

Very little work has been done on AI requirements testing yet. As agents write more of the code, the part people write is the specification, and the work moves back toward writing it first, closer to waterfall. Testing that specification becomes the main job, and that is where this loop puts its effort.

On the slides: the cover, slide 6.
sections.idea:
The idea in one minute

When an AI agent writes code, it usually finishes by saying it is done. Most of the time you cannot check that without reading everything it did. The closed loop makes “done” something a machine can check.

Think of a building inspector with the plans in hand. The plans are your requirements, written down as data instead of as a paragraph. The inspector never takes the builder’s word. It checks every item on the plans against the building, and for every part of the building it asks which item on the plans that part is for.

What keeps the inspection honest is that the inspector also breaks things on purpose. It takes a piece of working code, changes it slightly so it is wrong, and checks that at least one test notices. If no test notices, nothing is really checking that code, whatever the test report says.

At the end you get a count of three things: breaks no test noticed, code no requirement asked for, and questions only the owner can answer. “Done” means that count is zero.

Why a count and not a feeling

“Did I think of every requirement?” has no answer: what you forgot leaves no trace. “Is the list of open questions empty?” does have one, because the list is generated from the plans and the code, not from memory. So the loop never tries to be complete by writing more. It walks the plans, and every gap it meets becomes a question with a file and a line.

On the slides: slide 6.
sections.why:
Why use it

Requirements written as prose cannot fail

A paragraph saying “the player can buy an item if they have enough money” never turns red when the code drifts away from it. The loop keeps each requirement as a record with an id, its source, and the code it points at, so a requirement that no longer matches the code shows up as a failure.

Tests can pass for the wrong reason

A test that checks the price shown on screen passes even if buying never takes the money out of the wallet. Every test is green and the rule is broken. Breaking the code on purpose finds this: take the line that subtracts the money out, and see whether any test fails. If none does, the rule has no test, however many tests there are.

Long runs forget

An agent’s working memory (its context window) fills up during a long job, and early details drop out. Later steps then guess at what was settled before. The loop writes everything it learns to a graph on disk, so a later step looks the answer up instead of guessing it again. Every entry says where it came from.

On the slides: slide 4.
sections.when:
When it fits, and when it does not

Use it for larger systems: code that many changes will touch, where a rule must still be true after the agent’s tenth edit as well as its first, and where you want to know which line exists because of which requirement. It also helps most when agents run for hours, across many context windows.

Skip it for a one-off prompt, a quick script, or exploring an idea. The loop costs setup and run time, and it pays that back only when the same requirements are held across many changes. It is also no help with how something looks or feels: visuals, timing and feel still need a person.

On the slides: slide 25.
sections.thin:
Why a thin model can be worse than nothing

The loop can only check what is written in the model. Suppose the model holds three requirements and two tests. The loop may honestly report everything closed, because everything it knows about is checked. But a green report reads as “the work is complete”, when all it proves is that three small things are right. That false confidence is worse than having no report at all.

How large a model must be before its report means something is only partly known. The first measurements are in Seed it first, then it flies. Until there are more, treat a green loop over a small model as “these few things hold”, never as “it is done”.

Open How many requirements, tests and graph nodes are “enough” for the whole report is not known yet; for the part that learns there is a first answer.

On the slides: slide 25, slide 25.
sections.seed:
Seed it first, then it flies

The loop learns from what is already written down. Give it a model with a handful of requirements and it can check those few, but it has little to reason from when new code arrives. Give it many, with their code claimed, and it starts to see the patterns: which requirement a new branch most likely belongs to, which questions follow from which. So the order of work is: seed the model with as many sourced requirements as you can, then let the loop carry it.

How full is full enough

We measured this for the part that learns, the graph neural network (GNN). For each graph it was allowed to see only a share of the known links between code and the requirements that own it (a tenth, a quarter, half, three quarters, all of them), always tested on methods it had never seen, and compared with a plain rule that does not learn: “suggest the requirements whose effects already sit in this method”.

Where these numbers come from

Measured The two kit examples (4 requirements each): the plain rule wins at every fullness, 0.90 and 0.86 against the graph neural network (GNN)’s best of 0.78 and 0.85.

Measured The tool’s own model (20 requirements): the graph neural network (GNN) wins only at half and falls back after, so it has no dependable crossover yet.

Measured The largest graph measured, a game feature of ours that is not public: the GNN lost below half the links and won from half on, against the same plain rule. No count is given because the feature is not public, and the curve has not been drawn on the public targets here.

Two seeds each, five folds by method, 29 October. That is thin: read it as a first shape, not a law.

So on a small model the GNN stays quiet and the plain rule does the work. Where it has earned its place, it did so only on the largest graph, and only once about half of its code was claimed.

Some requirements are pillars

Which requirements are written matters as much as how many. A few carry most of the code. On osu!’s scoring rules, 13 of its 30 requirements own 80% of the branches a requirement owns, and the top three own 28%; on SemVer 11 of 19 own 80% and the top three 37%; on JsonObject 9 of 27 own 80% and the top three 46%. On the tool’s own model, 7 of the 12 requirements that own any code own 80% of it, and one of them runs through 16 methods. Seed those first: a rule that runs through many methods gives the rest of the graph something to attach to.

The same curve was then seeded by requirement instead of by method: only some requirements' claims were seen, added in three orders.

Where these numbers come from

Measured On the largest graph, the game feature of ours: the GNN beat the plain rule in random order only once every requirement was seeded. Seeded pillars first (the requirements owning the most code) it won from about a quarter of the requirements, and seeded cross-cutting first (the requirements running through the most methods) it won from the first three. No counts are given because the feature is not public.

Measured On the tool's own model (20 requirements) no order makes the GNN beat the plain rule.

One seed each, five folds by method, 29 October. Thin, but the gap between the orders was large.

So which requirements are written first matters more than how many. On the one graph it won on, the few that run through the most methods gave the learning part what a random start needed nearly all of them for. Write the cross-cutting rules first.

The smallest seed that grows into the whole loop

The loop already grows requirements. It walks each step, asks what the step needs, and every need nobody wrote becomes a new requirement for the owner to settle. On SemVer, 3 of the 19 requirements are marked inferred that way, on top of the 16 that cite the spec. So the open question is how small the written set can be and still grow into the full model. A small, well-chosen seed would mean less to write up front, and a structure that is easier to keep consistent.

Open The experiment for it: give an agent only the problem story and a few pillar requirements, let it grow the model with the loop, and count how many of the full model’s requirements it arrives at, and at what cost.

sections.how:
How to run it

  1. Install. python install.py puts the skill where Claude Code finds it and the tools beside it, then runs every selftest and the whole loop on a small example project. The example must pass (“hold”), or the install says so. See Install.
  2. Write the model of your system. First the problem story in your own words, each sentence with its source. Then the requirements, each pointing at the code it is about. Then the use cases: who wants what, step by step. Then a short block that names your code folders and your test files. python -X utf8 usecase_model.py <model> checks the 19 rules (see The model).
  3. Run the one command. 
    CLOSED_LOOP_ROOT=<your repo> python -X utf8 closed_loop.py run <model> --out REPORT.md --pin-claims "<why>"
    It breaks your code every way it knows, runs your tests against every break, builds the graph, applies the 18 checks and writes a report.
  4. Close what is yours. The report sorts what is open into two kinds. Yours: a missing test, a line no requirement claims, a break that changes nothing and needs explaining. The owner’s: questions about what the system should do, which only the person who owns the requirements can answer.
  5. Take the lock. When nothing of yours is left, --accept "<why>" records the verified state. A later change to that code makes the affected requirements stale until they are verified again. The lock refuses while any hole of yours stands, so it can never be used to turn a red report green.

sections.ten:
The ten points, each with its section

  1. What it is: one command that holds an agent’s requirements to the code, the tests and the agent’s own reasoning. More
  2. How it tests: it breaks every decision in the code on purpose, every way it knows, and each break must make a test fail, the test of the requirement that owns that code. More, the right test
  3. Speed: every break is built in one compile, then each runs alone. More
  4. The graph is the record: every piece is a node, and the checks read the graph. More
  5. Three trials on code you can read: breaks caught, bugs run, and a control run without the loop. More
  6. Equivalents: a break that changes nothing is proven or explained, never waved away. More
  7. The test subjects: a published spec, a JSON object and a shipped game’s scoring rules, each chosen for a reason. More
  8. The GNN: a learning model that suggests which requirement owns new code. More
  9. On against off: the same task given to two agents, one using the loop, graded blind. More
  10. A fresh reviewer each pass: a new agent hunts for ways a check could pass wrongly. More

sections.speed:
Why it is fast enough

Building each broken copy separately would mean hundreds of compiles. Instead, every method is copied once per break inside one build, and a switch picks which copy runs. One compile serves every break. A copy that does not compile is found by the line and column of its error and dropped, and the rest are rebuilt.

Each break then runs the tests alone, in its own copy of the build in a temporary folder. The live project is never touched.

Where these numbers come from

Measured On 30 October a whole pass took about 13 minutes on SemVer (246 breaks), about 9 on JsonObject (582) and about 74 on osu!’s scoring rules (563), each break run alone in a copy of the project, two at a time, at low priority on a busy machine. osu! is slow because every break of a constructor rebuilds the game.

On the slides: slide 3, slide 9.
sections.claims:
Claims and locks

A claim says “this method belongs to requirement X”. The loop pins each claim to a fingerprint of the method’s statements. If someone adds a line to that method or deletes one, the fingerprint changes and the claim goes stale. A new line can never slip in under an old claim without being looked at.

The pins are kept in a small file (claims.lock). If that file goes missing, every claim is unpinned until a person pins them again with a reason. A missing lock never quietly re-pins itself; a reviewer found that it used to, and it was fixed.

On the slides: slide 9, slide 21.
sections.criteria:
The 18 checks

Each check is named after the mistake it stops. Each one is proven by a planted mistake: the tool’s own selftest builds a small model with that exact mistake in it and requires the check to catch it. A check that has only ever passed cannot be told apart from one that is switched off.

L1Identity. Things keep their identity across rebuilds, so a verdict never ends up attached to the wrong thing.
L2Sourced. Every requirement traces to something outside the model: a person’s words, a design document. Nothing is invented.
L3Corroborated. A requirement only one source states is listed, because it inherits that source’s mistakes.
L4Carried. Every requirement is reached by some path through the main use case. Otherwise nobody builds it.
L5Ended. Every path has an end and someone acting; every step carries something.
L6Answered. Every question was answered by a person, not settled by a guess.
L7Realized. Code linked to a requirement has the shape the requirement describes.
L8Falsifiable. A check must be able to fail. One that passes whatever the code does is a hole.
L9Justified. Code no requirement asked for is flagged: behaviour that slipped in.
L10Defined. A requirement names things the code really has, and uses each word one way.
L11Causal. Every step’s starting condition is made true by something earlier.
L12Consistent. No two requirements demand opposite things.
L13Change-safe. A requirement, or the code it reads, that changed after it was verified is stale until verified again.
L14Caught. Breaking a requirement’s code makes a test fail.
L15Pinned. Every branch is held by a test: break it any way and something fails.
L16Own check. The test that notices is the requirement’s own named test (why).
L19Equivalent. A break called “the same program” has a proof, or a reason no test refutes (why).
L20Documented. A document that names a requirement the model does not hold, or an authored link that no longer stands, is a hole. A requirement no document describes is listed, not failed (why).

The numbering skips L17 and L18. L17 is a planned check from the research (vacuity: a requirement’s check must fail when its condition is forced off), not built yet.

On the slides: slide 8.
sections.modal:
Must and may: what “closed” means

The research behind the loop looked at how logicians describe “complete”. The closest fit is a Modal Transition System (Larsen and Thomsen, 1988). Every behaviour is marked either must (it has to happen) or may (it is allowed, not yet decided). A specification is finished when no “may” is left: every open choice has been settled one way or the other.

Here, the authored requirements are the musts. The inferred ones, the things the steps need that nobody wrote, are the mays. Each may is a question for the owner, who settles it as a must or as “either is fine”. On SemVer, “Parse throws on exactly the strings TryParse refuses” is one such may: the spec says what is valid, not how a class refuses, and no one has said.

The honest limit

Breaking code can show that requirements are not closed. It can never prove they are. “Closed” always means “closed against the breaks we tried and the tests that watched”. A new kind of break might find something new.

On the slides: slide 11.
sections.goalslist:
Two lists: what they train for, and what they could train with

Goals are how we understand what we are training for, and trying for a goal does not mean reaching it. So every goal is listed with what it was measured against and whether it got there, beside a second list: every stat and piece of metadata on file, what it does today, and which goals use it. The two work on each other through the node graph. A goal that loses to a plain rule asks for what stands behind that rule as an input. A stat no goal reads is a possible input, or something worth predicting. A relation in the graph that nothing predicts is a goal on offer.

Tried, and did not work: a goal as a vector

Measured We turned each goal into a list of numbers measured before training and fitted a direction to what paid off, then tested it on graphs it had never seen, with its bars and predictions committed first. There is a weak direction for what a network can learn, and none for what saves work. The two point about 95 degrees apart. Copying a goal's sources could game it, and it ranked a random relation high. It rests on 13 graphs in 5 domains, so it can show a direction is not general, not that none exists.

Measured What did hold: goals where each answer belongs to about one source beat a plain rule far more often, right 80% of the time against a 48% base, on 44 goals across 5 graphs. And ordering tests by a plain rule already saves most of what ordering them can: a learned order beat it on 2 of 10 goals.

Both lists are generated from the records, a job no goal claims fails the check, and each run logs what moved. See the Goals List and the Stats List.
sections.reviewers:
A fresh reviewer every pass

After each pass, a new agent that has not seen the work is asked one question: how could each check pass while the requirement is not really closed? A fresh agent is used because one that built the work tends to confirm it.

What they found

Measured The first reviewer found 9 such ways, all fixed. The second found 10; 8 are fixed and 2 are open. Three examples:

  • Deleting a line made the score better. Now the claim’s fingerprint moves and the claim goes stale (claims).
  • Naming more tests as a requirement’s checks could only remove holes. Now a named test must catch a break of its own requirement (the right test).
  • A deleted lock file re-pinned itself in silence. Now a missing lock leaves every claim unpinned.

Open A structured claim on each reasoning step (so a step that says “or” where the code says “and” fails), and the on/off pair rerun with a hidden acceptance test (on against off).

Every fix lands with a planted mistake the selftest must catch, the same rule as for the 18 checks.

On the slides: slide 21.
sections.buzzsaw:
Buzzsaw testing: attacking the assumptions

Breaking the code attacks the code. Buzzsaw testing attacks what the requirements assume. Every model takes some things as given:

  • Inferred requirements: things a step needs that nobody wrote down. Only the owner can say if they are right.
  • Entry conditions: facts that come from outside the model, such as “the string a caller hands in”.
  • Declared equivalents: breaks someone said change nothing, with a reason.

For each one, buzzsaw flips the answer (“what if this is not true?”) and walks the graph to find everything that rests on it: the later steps of every use case that relies on it, the requirements those steps carry, their effects, the code, and the tests that would have to change. That set is the assumption’s blast radius. The widest ones go to the owner first, because the most depends on them.

Measured on the public trials

Measured SemVer: 11 assumptions, 3 inferred requirements and 8 entry conditions, and the owner’s widest question reaches a radius of 7. JsonObject: 19, 6 inferred and 13 entry conditions, the widest question a radius of 57. osu!: 15, all entry conditions, with no inferred requirement and so no question to rank.

A lesson from building it

The first version said every assumption reached nearly every step and every test, so it could not rank anything. The summary use case (the epic) repeats requirements the detailed use cases carry, and walking on from the summary reaches everything. Starting the walk only from the most specific step that carries an assumption fixed it.

What it cannot do: it does not know which answer is right, and it measures how much depends on an assumption, not how likely it is to be wrong. Next: the same attack on the values a model takes from outside, by changing each value across its range and running the tests (Open).
sections.feature:
The test subjects

Every number in this manual comes from code you can read, or from the toolkit’s own source. Three subjects were chosen, each for a reason.

  • Unreal Engine’s SemVer parser is the academic one. A published spec, Semantic Versioning 2.0.0, says exactly what the class must do, so every requirement can cite a numbered rule. It has 68 statements and 2 tests.
  • Unreal Engine’s JsonObject has a contract from three places: its own doc comments, Microsoft’s published Equals and GetHashCode contract, and RFC 8259. It has 289 statements and 43 tests.
  • osu!’s scoring rules are the game: a shipped open-source rhythm game (ppy/osu, MIT), held to its own doc comments, with the 151 test cases of three test files. It has 191 statements.

No code was changed and no test or product code was written: only a requirements model for each, and /// CHECKS: comments in a scratch copy of the tests. The numbers, the bugs and how to re-run them are in on code you can read for yourself. The kit’s own example, a store’s wallet, is the one every install runs.

On the slides: slide 3, slide 14.
sections.self:
The tool runs on itself

The loop’s own requirements are written as a model too, from the author’s own words with their dates: 7 use cases, 18 authored requirements and 2 inferred ones, and the model passes the 19 rules. A Python adapter breaks the loop’s own decision code the same way the C# adapter breaks a game’s, and the loop’s selftests are the tests.

The model is expected to stay open in places, and to say so: it must report that the installer is the newest piece, that the two targets are not measured, and that a reviewer every pass is still a practice rather than a check.

The first pass on its own code (29 October, 65 minutes)

Measured 1,626 breaks of the tool’s own decision code. Its selftests caught 885 (54%); 647 got past every test; 94 were proven to change nothing by comparing compiled bytecode. 174 of 392 statements are held by a test (44%).

So the tool is less tested than SemVer (71% of its statements held, against its own 44%) and than JsonObject (61%), and about as tested as osu!’s scoring rules under three test files (42%). Its tests are planted mistakes that each prove one rule; they were never written to catch every break of every line. That gap is the next work, and these numbers are on code you will hold: the kit ships this source.

Measured The model passes all 19 rules; its graph holds 2,335 nodes and 6,259 edges; 2 questions stay open for the owner.

Two lessons from getting it to run

The first attempt ran all 1,626 breaks, then crashed while writing the summary, and the hour of runs was lost. The tool now saves every verdict before it builds the summary, and reuses them when the code and tests are unchanged. The second attempt refused to start, correctly, because a tool’s own test was failing while it was being edited. Rule since: never edit a tool while a run is using it.

On the slides: slide 21.
sections.public:
A run on public code: the asteroids mining loop

Numbers from a private repository are hard to trust from outside. So the loop also ran on a game whose code anyone can read: the asteroids mining loop of starfighter, a browser game in JavaScript. Its repository already holds a use-case document for the mining loop (ASTEROID_USE_CASES.md) and the list of the 61 constants that govern rocks, gems, the belt and the mining drones.

The kit cannot break JavaScript yet (it has adapters for C# and Python), so this run uses only the parts that do not need the code broken: the model’s 19 rules, the graph, the checks that read only the graph, buzzsaw and the question grid. The model says so itself, and the other checks report “not held” rather than passing.

Measured

Measured The document became 7 use cases and 48 requirements: 44 traced to the code, 4 open questions for the owner. All 61 constants are claimed by some step.

Measured 10 requirements rest only on what a function does (for example “a destroyed rock spills a gem”), with no constant behind them. The constant list cannot see them; only breaking the code could hold them. That is exactly where a JavaScript adapter would pay.

Measured Of the checks that need no code: 10 requirements with no source standing behind them, 34 resting on a single source, 4 open questions, and none carried by nothing or ending nowhere. Buzzsaw ranks the owner’s first question as “which collision applies ramming damage?”: five later steps rest on it.

Measured The tool’s own cross-check found a row in the document with a missing column before anything else ran.

A thin graph, on purpose

The graph holds 186 nodes and 396 edges, with no code and no tests in it. That is the thin case this manual warns about (why): the checks that ran are real, but a clean result here would mean little, and the GNN has nothing to learn from.
sections.telemetry:
Telemetry: measuring growth both ways

A loop can look better by trying less, and look worse by trying more. So every number the loop records is one of five kinds, and they are read together:

Net
How hard the pass tried: how many breaks, how many kinds, how much code. Should grow, then hold.
Closure
How much of what it tried was caught, claimed or answered. Should grow towards the net.
Open
What is still open, and whose it is. Should shrink; the owner’s part only shrinks when the owner answers.
Cost
What a pass costs in time. Should not grow faster than the net.
Tool
The tool itself: its size, and how much of it its own planted mistakes prove.

A pass where the net grew and the open count grew too is progress, not a step back. The list of stats is revisited every pass, and a new one is added whenever a pass shows growth the existing ones miss.

On the slides: slide 21.
sections.choose:
How the stats choose what to improve next

Every pass, each stat in the morph log is read as a trend over the passes and given one word: improving, worsening, stalled (the last three values barely moved), done (an open count stuck at zero), or too few (fewer than three passes have it). The word compares the stat to the way its kind should move: the net and what was caught should rise, what is open should fall.

The next improvement is then chosen by the stats, not by a person’s feeling. Each area of the tool (tests, the GNN, the kinds of break, speed, the owner’s questions, assumptions, coverage) names the stats that speak for it. A worsening stat scores 3, a stalled one 2, and an area scores its worst stat. The GNN tune is also due every five passes. The pick, and the trend lines that chose it, are printed after every pass.

What the first picks were

Measured Over its first recorded passes the graph grew, and the stats’ first pick was the GNN tune, because it had never been run (the tune).

Measured A bug the selftest caught while building this: adding up an area’s stats ranked two related GNN stats, both stalled, above a survivor count that was getting worse. An area now scores its single worst stat.

Stats that might predict others

The loop also looks for stats that move before others: does a change in one stat this pass go with a change in another the next pass? Each pair says how many passes it rests on. With fewer than eight it is labelled an anecdote, and pairs where one stat is simply made from the other are labelled mechanical. Every pair so far rests on a handful of passes, so they are anecdotes to watch, not findings.

The report every 20 passes

Every 20th pass writes a report: each stat’s trend, how much the graph grew (in total and by kind of node) for the feature’s model and for the loop’s own requirements model, the predictive candidates, the GNN tunes so far, and what the stats pick next.
sections.learn:
What it can learn from its own stats

Every pass leaves a verdict for every break: which kind of break, on which statement, in which method, and whether a test caught it. That is training data. A small model trained on it ranks the breaks most likely to get past the tests first, so a pass can show its holes early, and an agent writing new code can be told where its tests are likely to be weak before anything runs.

The test that lets it improve

It is only scored on code it never saw: whole methods are held out, and the score is how many of the real survivors it finds in the first fifth of its ranking. Random order finds a fifth; the plain rule to beat ranks each kind of break by how often that kind survived before.

Where these numbers come from

Measured Within one game feature of ours, the learner found more of the survivors in the first fifth than the plain rule did, at every one of ten seeds; no count is given because the feature is not public.

Measured Within the tool's own code: 30% over ten seeds, against the plain rule's 25% (random 20%). It won at nine of the ten, and the first seed happened to be the one it lost.

Measured Across projects it is worse than random: the words it learns belong to one project. Only the plain rule carries over. So, again: seed first, then it flies.

The real test of learning is over time: trained on the earlier passes, scored on the next pass's new code. That needs every pass's verdicts kept; until 29 October each pass overwrote the last, so the loop now archives them, and that test starts with the next passes.

Planned rounds of improvement

The standing loop works in epochs of twelve ticks. The first tick of an epoch is a brainstorm: a fresh agent reads the stats, the tick log and the results, and ranks ideas by the one stat each should move. The last tick is a benchmark: the same fixed measures every time, on inputs no tick may change. An epoch counts as an improvement only if a number moved the right way and none moved the wrong way.

The code-writing side

Planned Connect what it learns to the agent that writes the code: before it writes tests, hand it the statements of its change most likely to get past them, and the requirement the GNN thinks its new method belongs to. Measured as a third arm beside on and off.
sections.novelty:
How new is it?

An independent agent with web search compared the loop with published work on 29 October. Its answer: about eight of the ten parts are known. Requirements kept as data with gaps turned into questions are close to GitHub's Spec Kit and to Kiro's requirements turned into tests. Compiling all breaks at once and checking only what changed is what Stryker.NET already does. Breaks as feedback to an AI agent is Meta's mutation-guided test generation. Suggesting which requirement owns code is standard trace-link recovery.

Medium confidence What looks new is the whole used as an agent's "done" gate: every break in requirement-owned code must be caught by that requirement's own test, proven to change nothing by compiled code, explained with a reason that lapses when its code changes, or settled by the owner. Pieces of that exist (TestSuiteBench ties each break to one requirement and one test); the gate does not seem to.

It also said three things are aimed slightly off, and each could change the outcome more than polish: the breaks are syntactic while agents' mistakes are about intent; the on/off test graded correctness, where both sides hit the ceiling, rather than the tests left behind; and the GNN ignores its strongest signal, which requirement's tests catch the new code's breaks. The second is now measured (six kinds of task); the other two are on the work board.
sections.adapters:
Other languages

The model, the graph, the checks, the GNN and the telemetry do not care what language the code is in. Only the part that breaks code does:

  • C#: any .NET project, through dotnet test.
  • Python: breaks code through its syntax tree; the tests are commands.
  • Anything else (C++, Blueprints): write an adapter that produces one result file in the same format the C# adapter writes: for each requirement, whether its code has the right shape, and for each break, whether a test caught it and which.

On the slides: slide 27.
sections.harness:
The harness matters more than the prompt

Most of the gain is in how the agents are set up, not in what they are asked. The loop is a harness: a model to act on, checks that can fail, a record that outlives the context window, fresh reviewers, and measurements of its own progress. Keep improving your own: the agents’ instructions, their tools, and what they must prove before they say “done”. Measure each change with the on/off harness rather than by feel.

What would help most in return:

  • Benchmarks: agents with and without it, on your own systems.
  • Failure piles: the kinds of failure you see, and how often.
  • A wrong pass: any check you can make pass for the wrong reason.

On the slides: slide 27.
sections.glossary:
Words used here

Break (mutant)
A copy of the code changed on purpose so it is wrong.
Caught (killed)
A break that made at least one test fail. Good.
Got past (survived)
A break every test still passed. A missing test, unless it is equivalent.
Equivalent
A break that does not change what the program does.
Requirement
One rule the system must follow, with an id, a source and the code it points at.
Authored / inferred
Written by a person / found missing by the loop. Inferred ones are questions.
Use case
Who wants what, as numbered steps.
Claim
“This code belongs to that requirement.”
Lock
The recorded, verified state. A later change makes what it touches stale.
Node, edge
A thing in the graph, and a link between two things.
Check (criterion)
One of the 18 rules the graph is held to, each named after the mistake it stops.
Planted mistake
A deliberate error the selftest makes to prove a check can fail.
Must / may
Decided / not yet decided by the owner.
MRR
A score for a ranking: 1 for right-first, ½ for second, ⅓ for third, averaged.
Arm
One of the two agents in an on/off pair.
Acceptance test
A test written before the arms start and hidden from both.
Morph log
The file that gets one line of numbers per pass.
